author: Tom Huntington Arts Correspondent
title: Jeff Tweedy's 'Twilight Override': Wilco frontman serves up intimate magnum opus | Rutland Reader | rutlandherald.com
text:
Inspired by a road trip with his sons Spencer and Sammy at the outset of the pandemic and the related trauma he says we’re still dealing with, Jeff Tweedy set out to make something special for his next solo album.
“What I really want to do is grow my heart big enough to love everyone,” states Tweedy, a prolific songwriter and frontman of celebrated Chicago-based band Wilco, in press materials. “And if I want a heart big enough to meet this moment, it requires something expansive.”
That something is Tweedy’s new triple album, “Twilight Override,” released last week on Wilco’s dBpm Records label.
Tweedy’s fifth solo album, the epic 30-song set is actually a collaborative effort that features Tweedy and his homespun band of friends and family: James Elkington (guitar), Liam Kazar (bass, vocals, guitar), Sima Cunningham (piano, vocals) and Macie Stewart (violin, vocals) along with Spencer Tweedy (drums, vocals) and Sammy Tweedy (synthesizers, vocals).
All but Elkington will be on hand for Tweedy’s two area tour stops, a sold-out show on Oct. 13 at Higher Ground (with Cunningham opening) and Oct. 14 at Lebanon Opera House (with Stewart opening).
“I mean, what else do I have but my songs and my family and my friends?” adds Tweedy. “How else can I generate my own light?”
“To me, any song, no matter the subject matter, can be a point of light and that’s one of the reasons I try and make so many of them. They all have the potential … to lift someone up.”
Recorded at Wilco’s Chicago studio The Loft, “Twilight Override” is a reflective, mostly acoustic guitar-based collection that delivers plenty of spirit-lifting moments. Spanning three discs and clocking in at just under two hours, it encourages listeners to slow down and immerse themselves in the deeply compelling material.
Full of beautifully intimate, earnest and compassionate ruminations on the human condition, and enhanced throughout with stellar vocal harmonies and deft instrumentation by his tight-knit and sympatico band, “Twilight Override” finds Tweedy at the top of his game on the epic magnum opus.
“Taken together, these 30 tracks amplify and enrich each other, adding up to a whopper of an album that rewards the time you spend with it,” said Rolling Stone, calling it “a many-splendored marvel.”
‘The best I can do’
“Twilight Override” opens with the meditative “One Tiny Flower,” an improvised six-minute song with poetic lyrics and moody instrumentation. And Tweedy employs his spoken voice on the dreamlike “Parking Lot,” another poem-based tune.
The upbeat and infectious “Forever Never Ends” kicks things up a notch with Tweedy’s nostalgic tale of an ill-fated high-school prom night that’s set to a jangly roots-rock soundtrack and his searing electric guitar work.
Other highlights of the first record include the hypnotic “Love is for Love,” the loping “Betrayed” and the poignant closer, “Throwaway Lines.”
“I was born a little sad / Never knew what I had,” sings Tweedy on the pretty “KC Rain (No Wonder),” which kicks off the second disc. “New Orleans” is a gorgeous standout with spellbinding guitar work by Tweedy, while the hushed and enigmatic “Blank Baby” uses the group’s impressive vocal harmonies to great effect.
And the closing “Feel Free” is a subdued seven-minute centerpiece song that finds Tweedy more assured than ever, delivering evocative mantra-like verses with aplomb.
Disc three comes roaring out of the gate with the supercharged and catchy “Lou Reed Was My Babysitter,” a tune originally intended for Wilco, while the stripped-down title track pairs mesmerizing lyrics with delicate instrumentation.
And the buoyant closer “Enough” is a hopeful paean to people who keep on keeping on in the face of life’s travails.
“I think this one is special, a really beautiful evolution,” Tweedy told Mojo magazine about “Twilight Override,” calling it “a big open-hearted outpouring” and “the defining statement of my solo career so far.”
“I’m not holding back or protecting myself, and I don’t care if people think a triple record’s too long.”
Tweedy says the three records “represent the past, present, and future,” calling them “a response to the feeling that we’re stuck in the worst part of the day, saying goodbye to the future we woke up to, waiting for it to get dark enough to dream up a new day.”
“In all these songs, I’m dreaming,” he says. “Of who I once was, who you are now, who we could be.”
“Truthfully, I’ve been doing this for a long time,” adds Tweedy. “And I’m not going anywhere. This is the stuff that works for me. Feeling free. Making records with my friends and adding my voice to a song that never ends.”
“Sharing this music with the world is the best I can do.”
